title: From Problem to Program
summary: This unit shows how problems can be described using functions (Funktion) and precise algorithms (Algorithmus). The Euclidean algorithm (euklidischer Algorithmus) illustrates recursion (Rekursion), base cases (Rekursionsanker), and termination (Termination). The unit then introduces core MiniJava constructs such as variables (Variable), assignments (Wertzuweisung), input/output (Eingabe/Ausgabe), selection (Selektion), blocks (Blöcke), and iteration (Iteration).
keyFacts: Arithmetic operations can be modeled as functions, for example, addition as $f: Q \times Q \to Q$.
An algorithm is a precise description of how to produce a desired result from an input.
An algorithm also describes a sequence of individual process steps and can process or implement a function.
Not every function is computable; this question belongs to computability theory.
The Euclidean algorithm determines the greatest common divisor of two positive integers $a$ and $b$.
If $a=b$ holds, the base case has been reached and the algorithm returns $a$.
If $a>b$ holds, $a$ is replaced by $a-b$, and the algorithm returns to step 1.
If $a<b$ holds, $b$ is replaced by $b-a$, and the algorithm returns to step 1.
The Euclidean algorithm terminates because the values remain positive and eventually the base case is reached.
Static finiteness means that an algorithm's description has finite length.
Dynamic finiteness is associated with the termination of execution.
Variables have values that can be used as arguments to operations.
Variables declared inside `main` do not receive a default value and must be initialized.
An assignment changes the value stored in a variable.
MiniJava is used for the first exercises and at the beginning of the module.
`readInt` is used to read an integer, while `write` outputs a value.
`if`/`else` enables conditional selection; blocks group statements, and iteration means repeated execution.
Comments can explain a program; `javac` compiles it, and `java` runs it.

review.notes: 44 Fragen geprüft. Eine Cloze-Frage hatte mit „1“ einen nicht eindeutig falschen Distraktor, da der Wert bei bestimmten Eingaben tatsächlich 1 sein kann; dieser wurde durch $a+1$ ersetzt. Keine Fragen mussten entfernt werden.

questions.prompt: Which description applies to an algorithm?

options.text: A single value stored in a variable.
A precise description of how to produce a desired result from an input.
A list of all possible functions, regardless of their input.
A random sequence of outputs with no defined steps.

questions.explanation: An algorithm specifies precisely how to produce a desired result from an input. It does this by describing a sequence of individual process steps.

questions.prompt: A function takes two rational numbers as input and returns their sum as a rational number. Here, $\mathbb{Q}$ denotes the set of rational numbers, $\mathbb{N}_{>0}$ the positive natural numbers, and $\times$ an ordered pair of numbers. Which signature describes this function?

options.text: $f: \mathbb{Q} \to \mathbb{Q} \times \mathbb{Q}$
$f: \mathbb{N}_{>0} \to \{yes,no\}$
$f: \mathbb{Q} \times \mathbb{Q} \to \mathbb{Q}$
$f: \{yes,no\} \to \mathbb{N}_{>0}$

questions.explanation: The function takes a pair of rational numbers and returns their sum. Thus, its domain is $\mathbb{Q} \times \mathbb{Q}$ and its codomain is $\mathbb{Q}$.

questions.prompt: Which statements describe an algorithm? Select all that apply; more than one may be correct.

options.text: It consists of a sequence of individual process steps.
Every mathematically described function can automatically be computed.
It can process or implement a function $f$.
It precisely describes how a desired result is produced from an input.

questions.explanation: An algorithm connects an input and a desired result through a precise sequence of process steps. However, it is not true that every function can be computed.

questions.prompt: Every function can be computed.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Not every function can be computed. This limitation is studied in computability theory.

questions.prompt: In the Euclidean algorithm, when $a=b$ is reached, $\gcd(a,b)=___$.

options.text: a-b
a
a+b

questions.explanation: When $a=b$ holds, the base case has been reached; the algorithm stops and returns $a$.

questions.prompt: What is the base case of the Euclidean algorithm?

options.text: $a=b$
$a<b$
$a>b$

questions.explanation: The base case is the condition $a=b$. At that point, no further calculation is performed; the current value is returned.

questions.prompt: What happens in the recursion step when $a>b$ holds?

options.text: $a$ is replaced by $a-b$, and the algorithm returns to step 1.
The algorithm immediately returns $b$.
$b$ is replaced by $b-a$, and the algorithm stops.
1 is added to each of $a$ and $b$.

questions.explanation: When $a>b$ holds, the larger value $a$ is replaced by the positive difference $a-b$. The check then starts again at step 1.

questions.prompt: What does static finiteness mean for an algorithm?

options.text: Every function can be computed by the algorithm.
All variables always have positive values.
Execution repeats every step infinitely many times.
The algorithm's description has finite length.

questions.explanation: Static finiteness concerns the description itself: it has finite length.

questions.prompt: Dynamic finiteness concerns the completion of an execution.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: In this course, dynamic finiteness is associated with termination, that is, with the end of an execution.

questions.prompt: A variable declared inside `main` can be safely used without being defined first.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Variables inside `main` do not receive a default value. They must be defined before they are used.
`x` is assigned the value 3. The assignment then calculates $3+19=22$, and `write` outputs 22.

questions.prompt: What value does the Euclidean algorithm return for $a=18$ and $b=12$?
questions.explanation: First, $18$ is replaced by $18-12=6$. Then $12$ is replaced by $12-6=6$; the algorithm ends when $a=b=6$ holds.

questions.prompt: After `x = 7; result = x;`, `result` has the value 7, while `x` remains unchanged.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: The current value of `x` is stored in `result`. Assigning a value to `result` does not change `x`.
The condition $4>9$ is false, so the `else` branch is executed. There, $9-4=5$ is calculated.

questions.prompt: Which mapping of MiniJava commands is correct?

options.text: `readInt` outputs a value, and `write` reads an integer.
Both commands declare variables.
Both commands repeat part of a program.
`readInt` reads an integer, and `write` outputs a value.

questions.explanation: `readInt` is used for input, while `write` is used for output. They therefore serve different roles in the program.

questions.prompt: What is conditional selection using `if` and `else` called?

options.text: Selection
Comment
Assignment
Iteration

questions.explanation: In selection, a condition determines which branch is executed. `if` and `else` form such a conditional choice.

questions.prompt: What value does the Euclidean algorithm return for $a=15$ and $b=6$?
questions.explanation: $15>6$, so $a$ becomes 9 and then 3. Next, $b$ becomes $6-3=3$; the base case returns 3.

questions.prompt: In the Euclidean algorithm, after replacing the larger value, the process returns to step 1.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: After replacing $a$ when $a>b$ holds, and after replacing $b$ when $a<b$ holds, the process continues at step 1.

options.text: The last assignment changes `x` to 26.
`result` has the value 26.
`x` has the value 7.
`result` remains 7 permanently.

questions.explanation: `x` remains 7, while the last assignment uses the current value of `x` and sets `result` to $7+19=26$.

questions.prompt: Which order is correct for compiling and running a MiniJava program?

options.text: First run it with `java`, then compile it with `javac`.
First output variables, then describe the algorithm.
First compile it with `write`, then run it with `readInt`.
First compile it with `javac`, then run it with `java`.

questions.explanation: The process described is to compile with `javac` and then run with `java`.

questions.prompt: `if`/`else` selects a branch based on a condition and is therefore a form of ___.

options.text: Comment
Selection
Assignment
Iteration

questions.explanation: Selection chooses between possible execution paths based on a condition.

questions.prompt: What are blocks used for in MiniJava?

options.text: They make every function computable.
They replace all variables with default values.
They group statements, for example in `if` or loop statements.
They automatically read an integer.

questions.explanation: Blocks group multiple statements together. This allows statements to belong together in an `if` branch or a loop.

questions.prompt: What value does the Euclidean algorithm return for $a=48$ and $b=18$?
questions.explanation: The values evolve as shown in $(48,18)\to(30,18)\to(12,18)\to(12,6)\to(6,6)$. At the base case, 6 is returned.

questions.prompt: Which observations explain why the Euclidean algorithm terminates? Select all that apply; more than one may be correct.

options.text: The values of $a$ and $b$ remain positive.
The larger value being replaced is replaced by a smaller positive difference.
After at most one step, $a=b$ always holds.
The values are never changed during execution.

questions.explanation: The values remain positive, and the larger value decreases at each step. Therefore, the base case $a=b$ is eventually reached, though not necessarily after a single step.

questions.prompt: Which pairing of base case and recursion step is correct?

options.text: Base case: $a<b$; step: add the two values.
Base case: $a=b$; step: replace the larger value with the difference and return to step 1.
Base case: read the input; step: output the result.
Base case: $a>b$; step: always stop immediately.

questions.explanation: The base case is the equality case. In all other cases, the larger value is reduced and the check is repeated.

questions.prompt: If $a\ne b$ holds in the Euclidean algorithm, it can already stop with $a$ as the GCD.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: The algorithm stops only at the base case $a=b$. If the values differ, further calculation is needed first.

questions.prompt: Why is it important to use parentheses correctly in an `if` construct?

options.text: Without parentheses, all variables are defined automatically.
Otherwise, the compiler may group or interpret statements differently from what was intended.
Parentheses replace the condition of the `if`.
Parentheses make `readInt` read random values.

questions.explanation: Incorrect parentheses can change which statements belong to a branch. As a result, the compiler may interpret a structure differently from what was intended.

questions.prompt: Which statements correctly distinguish the concepts of finiteness? Select all that apply; more than one may be correct.

options.text: Dynamic finiteness is associated with the termination of execution.
Static finiteness means that every result is the same.
Dynamic finiteness means that only finitely many variables appear in `main`.
Static finiteness means that the description has finite length.

questions.explanation: Static finiteness refers to the length of the description; dynamic finiteness refers to behavior during execution. Identical results or the number of declared variables do not define these concepts.

questions.prompt: What does the statement `result = x + 19;` mean in the variable model?

options.text: `result` is only checked for equality with `x`.
The statement ends the algorithm.
`x` is declared automatically and `result` is deleted.
The current value of `x` is used in the operation; the result is stored in `result`.

questions.explanation: The value of `x` can be used as an argument to addition. The calculated result is then stored in `result` by the assignment.
The condition $10>4$ is true. Therefore, the first branch is executed, and `result` is assigned the value $10-4=6$.

questions.prompt: Which pairing correctly connects each term to its execution behavior?

options.text: Selection and iteration: both are types of comments.
Selection and iteration: both are used only for output.
Selection: choosing based on a condition; iteration: repeated execution.
Selection: repeated execution; iteration: choosing based on a condition.

questions.explanation: Selection chooses an execution path based on a condition. Iteration means repeatedly executing part of a program.

questions.prompt: Comments execute a program's commands repeatedly.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Comments explain a program. They do not execute commands repeatedly.

questions.prompt: When using an `if` with multiple statements per branch, which measures help make the intended structure clear? Select all that apply; more than one may be correct.

options.text: Group a branch's statements in a block.
Omit blocks, because then all following statements automatically belong to the `if`.
Check which statements the compiler assigns to each branch.
Replace the condition with a comment.

questions.explanation: Blocks make the grouping of statements explicit. You should also check whether the branches are associated as intended.

questions.prompt: You want to implement the requirement “fastest route without stairs” for an ordered list in MiniJava. Which strategy matches the algorithm described?

options.text: If two routes take the same time, always replace the current route with the new one.
Always choose the shortest route, even if it has stairs.
If all routes have stairs, automatically choose the fastest route with stairs.
Ignore routes with stairs and store a route as `best` if none has been chosen yet or if it is faster.

questions.explanation: The requirement calls for a route without stairs. Therefore, routes with stairs are ignored, and a route is stored as the current choice only if none has been chosen yet or if it is faster than the current choice.

questions.prompt: A list contains $n$ routes. The current best route is stored, and each new route is checked once. Which runtime complexity matches this approach?

options.text: $T(n)=n\in\Theta(n)$
$T(n)=n^2\in\Theta(n)$
$T(n)=1\in\Theta(1)$
$T(n)=\frac{n(n+1)}{2}\in\Theta(n^2)$

questions.explanation: When the current best route is stored, each new route is checked exactly once. Therefore, $T(n)=n\in\Theta(n)$.

questions.prompt:
A route planner must select a route with no stairs. If no available route meets this requirement, it should output “No suitable route.” There are exactly two available routes: Route A takes 6 minutes and has stairs; Route B takes 9 minutes and has stairs.

Statement: The planner should output Route A because it is the fastest available route.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Both available routes have stairs, so neither meets the stated requirement. The planner should therefore output “No suitable route,” not Route A.

questions.prompt: What value does the Euclidean algorithm return for $a=84$ and $b=30$?
questions.explanation: The successive differences are shown in $(84,30)\to(54,30)\to(24,30)\to(24,6)\to(18,6)\to(12,6)\to(6,6)$. The base case returns 6.
The inputs set `x=11` and `y=4`. Since $11>4$ holds, the first branch is selected and $11-4=7$ is output.

questions.prompt: Which statements together provide a correct reason why the Euclidean algorithm is an algorithm in the sense described? Select all that apply; more than one may be correct.

options.text: For positive integers $a$ and $b$, it specifies a precise sequence of steps.
A finite description is not required for an algorithm.
At the base case, a value is returned as the greatest common divisor.
Termination depends on the values growing without bound.

questions.explanation: The algorithm specifies precise steps for the input and returns the GCD at the base case. A finite description is a required property of algorithms, and the values do not grow without bound.

options.text: `x` may only have the value 0.
`result` was not defined before it was used.
`write` can only output variables that were read using `readInt`.
A variable must never be used in `write`.

questions.explanation: Variables declared inside `main` do not receive a default value. Therefore, `result` must be defined before calling `write`.

questions.prompt: Which combinations correctly describe the development and execution of a MiniJava program? Select all that apply; more than one may be correct.

options.text: `write` creates comments in the program.
Comments can explain a program's purpose.
Blocks can group multiple statements in a branch.
`javac` compiles the program, and `java` runs it.
`readInt` replaces the compilation process.

questions.explanation: Blocks structure statements, comments explain code, and `javac` and `java` are used in the compilation and execution steps. By contrast, `readInt` and `write` are input/output commands.

questions.prompt: A procedure has a finite description but does not terminate for a particular input. Which statement is correct?

options.text: It satisfies static but not dynamic finiteness.
It satisfies both forms of finiteness.
It satisfies neither form because the description is finite.
It satisfies dynamic but not static finiteness.

questions.explanation: The finite description satisfies static finiteness. Since execution does not end, dynamic finiteness, or termination, is not satisfied in this case.
Since $2>5$ is false, `result` is first assigned $5-2=3$. The next assignment changes it to $3+19=22$.

questions.prompt: Which statements connect MiniJava constructs to their roles? Select all that apply; more than one may be correct.

options.text: `if` enables a choice based on a condition.
A comment repeatedly executes the program section it describes.
An assignment changes the value stored in a variable.
A variable's value can be used as an argument to an operation.
`write` declares a new variable.

questions.explanation: Variable values can be used in operations, `if` implements selection, and an assignment updates a stored value. Comments and `write` do not serve these roles.

levels.title: In Practice: Algorithms in Everyday Life

questions.prompt: You are driving through a city: your navigation system receives a starting point, destination, and traffic data, then calculates a route step by step. Which concept best describes this process?

options.text: Comment
Algorithm
Variable
Assignment

questions.explanation: An algorithm precisely describes process steps that produce a desired result from inputs. Here, the starting point, destination, and traffic data are the inputs, and the route is the output.

questions.prompt: A messaging app uses a key to transform a message into ciphertext according to fixed rules. Which concept is primarily involved?

options.text: Algorithm
Variable
Block
Base case

questions.explanation: Encryption consists of a precise sequence of processing steps, making it an algorithm. It processes the message and key as inputs and produces ciphertext as the result.

questions.prompt: You are testing a PIN checker: a PIN has exactly four digits, each digit can be from 0 to 9, and leading zeros are allowed. How many different PINs are there?
questions.explanation: Each of the four positions has 10 possibilities: $10^4=10\,000$. An algorithm can process this finite set of possible inputs for the PIN checker.

questions.prompt: You are programming a Sudoku solver and considering the successful solution case: it tries numbers and calls itself again for the smaller remaining problem. When is a suitable base case reached?

options.text: Another number is entered in a cell.
The Sudoku is completely and correctly filled in.
There is still an empty cell.
The next possible number is selected.

questions.explanation: In the successful solution case, the base case ends further calls once the goal is reached: the Sudoku is completely and correctly filled in. The recursion step, by contrast, handles a smaller remaining problem.

questions.prompt: Which two everyday situations clearly illustrate a conditional choice using `if`/`else`?

options.text: An upload is repeated until the server confirms receipt.
A variable is assigned the value `42`.
An ATM dispenses cash only if the PIN is correct; otherwise, it displays an error message.
A thermostat turns the heating on when the temperature is below a threshold, and off otherwise.

questions.explanation: In `if`/`else`, exactly one path is chosen based on a condition. The other examples illustrate iteration or assignment.

questions.prompt: A logic module has five independent yes/no inputs. How many rows are needed for a complete truth table covering every possible input combination?
questions.explanation: Each binary input doubles the number of combinations: $2^5=32$. The truth table thus represents a finite function for all possible inputs.

questions.prompt: An Excel-like spreadsheet initially contains `x = 7`. Then you set `x` to `26`. Which concept does this illustrate?

options.text: Base case
Assignment
Termination
Selection

questions.explanation: An assignment changes the value stored in a variable: `7` becomes `26`. The variable serves as a named storage location.

questions.prompt: You simulate the subtraction-based Euclidean algorithm for $(a,b)=(15,6)$. How many recursion steps occur before the base case is reached?
questions.explanation: The pairs are shown in $(15,6)\to(9,6)\to(3,6)\to(3,3)$. So there are three subtractions; then $a=b$ holds and the base case ends the algorithm.

questions.prompt: Is this correct: If `javac` translates a Java program into Java bytecode according to defined rules, an algorithm is at work.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: The translation follows a defined sequence of processing steps; this sequence is an algorithm. The input is the Java program, and, if translation succeeds, the output is Java bytecode.

questions.prompt: You want to reduce the fraction $84/30$ in an app. Which subproblem does the Euclidean algorithm solve directly?

options.text: Find the greatest common divisor of 84 and 30.
Read a PIN as input.
Find the shortest route between two places.
Encrypt a message.

questions.explanation: To reduce the fraction, you need the greatest common divisor: $gcd(84,30)=6$, so the fraction is divided by 6. The Euclidean algorithm finds this divisor through repeated steps that terminate.
